name: substrate-divergence-counterfactual
title: Mechanics-dominated counterfactual (positive control)
claim: In a MECHANICS-DOMINATED regime (strong differential adhesion + a strong chemoattractant gradient, no shared rules/ODE), the two substrates DIVERGE: the spatial equivalence test REJECTS equivalence (cross-backend spatial agreement 0.20 vs same-backend 1.00; TOST diff +0.80, margin +/-0.10). The divergence is mechanistically attributable -- the vertex fork's ActiveMigration climbs the gradient (type-A mean y 7 -> 17.9) while CPM's Metropolis chemotaxis barely moves it (y -> 10.7). This is the POSITIVE CONTROL for crossparadigm-equivalence: it proves the equivalence test can detect a real substrate difference, so the equivalence verdict on the Sego model is informative, not an artifact of an insensitive metric.
experiment: Run a mechanics-only blueprint (workspace/blueprints/mechanics_divergence.yaml: types A/B, A self-adhesive and repelled by B, a chemo field secreted by B with strong chemotaxis on A) on BOTH backends over rules-seeds {0,1,2} (N=80). Score the same-backend and cross-backend exact-position spatial agreement and apply the SAME metrics.equivalence_tost used by crossparadigm-equivalence (margin +/-0.10).
result: Spatial agreement: same-backend 1.000 (mechanics-only runs are deterministic per backend, so seeds reproduce exactly), cross-backend 0.20; TOST diff +0.80, far outside +/-0.10 -> NOT equivalent. Mechanistic cause: type-A cells migrate up the chemo gradient under the vertex ActiveMigration director (mean final y ~17.9 from a start of ~7) but barely move under CPM's Metropolis chemotaxis bias (y ~10.7), so the two substrates place the population very differently.

purpose.question: When MECHANICS (not the shared mechanism) drives the outcome, does the equivalence test correctly REJECT -- i.e. does it have the power to detect a real substrate difference?
purpose.mechanism: CPM moves cells by Metropolis acceptance of lattice copies (chemotaxis as an energy bias); the vertex fork moves them by the ActiveMigration director sampled from the field gradient. Under a strong gradient these displace cells by different amounts, and CPM's Potts neighbour-swapping sorts differentially- adhesive cells in a way the vertex topology resists -- so the spatial outcome genuinely depends on the substrate.
purpose.expected_outcome: Cross-backend spatial agreement well below the same-backend baseline; the TOST REJECTS equivalence.

key_assumptions: Mechanics-only (no rules/ODE/immune) so nothing shared forces agreement; the knobs are deliberately strong to enter a mechanics-dominated regime.
Nothing is tuned to hit a target; the study reports whatever the TOST returns (it rejected).
Same spatial metric + TOST + margin as crossparadigm-equivalence, so the two verdicts are directly comparable.

diagnose: If the test did NOT reject here, the metric/margin is too insensitive -- tighten before trusting any equivalence verdict.

limitations: An engineered extreme regime (deliberately strong adhesion + chemotaxis), chosen to make the substrate decisive -- not a biological claim about influenza.
Mechanics-only, so fate is static; the divergence is spatial/positional by construction.
Demonstrates the test's POWER and that mechanics-driven outcomes are substrate-sensitive; it does not quantify a biological effect size.

report.title: A mechanics-dominated regime where the substrates DIVERGE (test has power)
report.verdict: In a deliberately mechanics-dominated regime the substrates diverge: spatial equivalence is REJECTED (cross 0.20 vs same 1.00, TOST diff +0.80 vs +/-0.10), driven by a real migration difference (vertex A climbs the chemo gradient to y~17.9, CPM A stays near y~10.7). This is the positive control for the equivalence study: the same test that calls the Sego model fate-equivalent correctly rejects here, so that equivalence verdict is informative.
report.main_insight: The equivalence test is not rigged to say "equivalent": when mechanics drives the outcome, it detects the substrate difference. Substrate choice matters exactly when the mechanics (migration, sorting) -- not the shared mechanism -- sets the result.
report.caveat: An engineered extreme; mechanics-only (fate static). It demonstrates the test's power and substrate-sensitivity of mechanics-driven outcomes, not a biological effect size.

findings.statement: In a mechanics-dominated regime the spatial equivalence TOST REJECTS (cross 0.20 vs same 1.00, diff +0.80 vs margin 0.10), driven by a directed migration difference (vertex A to y~17.9, CPM A to y~10.7). The equivalence test can detect a real substrate difference, so crossparadigm-equivalence's positive verdict is informative, not an insensitivity artifact.

findings.explanation: Vertex ActiveMigration climbs the field gradient; CPM Metropolis chemotaxis barely moves cells at this strength, and Potts sorting differs from vertex topology.
findings.next_action: none -- serves as the positive control; could be swept over gradient strength to map where equivalence breaks.
